name: Semaglutide
evidenceNote: Approved by FDA for type 2 diabetes, weight management, heart risk reduction, kidney protection in diabetes, and a form of fatty liver disease, each on the strength of large randomized trials.
summary: Semaglutide is an FDA-approved GLP-1 drug, given weekly by injection or daily by tablet, for type 2 diabetes, weight loss, heart, kidney, and liver disease.
keyTakeaway: Semaglutide is a long-acting copy of GLP-1, a gut hormone that raises insulin after meals and dampens appetite. Novo Nordisk sells it as Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for weight management. In the 1,961-person STEP 1 trial, weekly injections cut body weight by 14.9% over 68 weeks versus 2.4% on placebo, and in SELECT they lowered heart attacks, strokes, and heart deaths by 20%. Its labels carry a boxed warning about thyroid tumors seen in rodents. Compounded copies lost their shortage exemption in 2025.

blocks.text: Semaglutide is a lab-made peptide that matches human glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) at 94% of its sequence. Natural GLP-1 lasts only minutes in the blood. Semaglutide is changed in two ways that stretch that to about a week: it resists the enzyme DPP-4 that normally destroys GLP-1, and it binds tightly to albumin, the main carrier protein in blood, which slows its clearance by the kidneys [1].

One molecule now sits behind several branded products. Ozempic began as the once-a-week diabetes pen, and since early 2026 the name also covers a once-daily tablet that sits alongside Rybelsus, the original oral version [1][3]. Wegovy is the weight-management brand, sold as a weekly injection, a higher-dose Wegovy HD injection, and a daily 25 mg tablet [2][9]. The doses and indications differ by product, so the brands are not interchangeable.
Semaglutide entered the US market for diabetes and then expanded, one outcome trial at a time, into weight, heart, kidney, and liver indications.

items.text: First US approval, as the weekly Ozempic injection for type 2 diabetes [1].
The STEP 1 trial reports 14.9% average weight loss with the 2.4 mg weekly dose [4].
SELECT shows fewer heart attacks, strokes, and cardiovascular deaths in people with obesity and heart disease but no diabetes [5].
FLOW shows slower kidney decline in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease [6].
FDA declares the semaglutide shortage resolved, ending the main legal basis for mass compounding [10].
Wegovy injection gains accelerated approval for MASH with moderate to advanced liver scarring [2].
Wegovy tablets are approved for weight management and heart risk reduction [2].
FDA approves Wegovy HD, a 7.2 mg weekly dose, after a 54-day review [9].

blocks.text: Semaglutide switches on the GLP-1 receptor, the same target as the body's own hormone. In the pancreas, this boosts insulin release and lowers glucagon release, but only when blood glucose is elevated, so on its own it rarely drives sugar too low [1]. It also slows the rate at which food leaves the stomach, which is why the labels warn that it can change how other oral medicines are absorbed [2].

The weight effect comes mainly from reduced hunger and calorie intake. GLP-1 receptors sit in several brain areas that regulate appetite, and in animal studies semaglutide reached and activated neurons in those regions [2]. Because the elimination half-life is about one week, the drug stays in circulation for roughly five weeks after the last dose [1]. That long tail is why the Wegovy label advises stopping at least two months before a planned pregnancy [2]. How it lowers cardiovascular risk has not been established [2].

Yes. Semaglutide has been FDA-approved since 2017 and now holds approvals across three product lines: Ozempic injection [1], Rybelsus and Ozempic tablets [3], and Wegovy injection and tablets [2]. The MASH indication is an accelerated approval, which means it rests on liver biopsy improvements and can be withdrawn if a confirmatory trial fails to show clinical benefit [2].

Compounded semaglutide is not FDA-approved. Pharmacies were allowed to make copies while the drug was officially in shortage. FDA ruled the shortage resolved on February 21, 2025, the grace period for state-licensed pharmacies has since ended, and as of April 2026 semaglutide is on neither the shortage list nor the 503B bulks list [10].

items: Blood sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes, as Ozempic injection or Rybelsus and Ozempic tablets [1][3].
Fewer major cardiovascular events (heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death) in type 2 diabetes with established heart disease or high cardiovascular risk [1][3].
Slower loss of kidney function, and fewer cases of kidney failure and cardiovascular death, when type 2 diabetes comes with chronic kidney disease [1].
Long-term weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and in children 12 and older with obesity (injection only) [2].
Fewer major cardiovascular events in adults with established heart disease who also have obesity or overweight [2].
Noncirrhotic MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, an inflammatory fatty liver disease) with stage F2 to F3 fibrosis, injection only [2].

blocks.text: Digestive effects lead the list. On Ozempic, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and constipation each affected at least 5% of patients [1]. In STEP 1 these were mostly mild to moderate and faded over time, but 4.5% of people on semaglutide stopped because of them, against 0.8% on placebo [4]. The Wegovy label adds headache, fatigue, dizziness, reflux, and hair loss to the common list, and notes that altered skin sensation was more frequent at the higher HD dose [2][9].

Every semaglutide label carries a boxed warning because the drug caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents; whether this happens in humans is unknown, and the drug is contraindicated when medullary thyroid cancer runs in the patient or their family, or with MEN 2 syndrome [1][2]. Other listed risks include pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, kidney injury from dehydration, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, worsening diabetic eye disease, a faster heart rate, serious allergic reactions, and food being inhaled into the lungs during anesthesia [2].
